title: The wolf of Gubbio (Little Flowers 21)
hook: a legend of Francis making peace between a wolf and a town

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis and Brother Leo on a winter road, and a locked gate. Your line was perfect joy. When something was refused you, what was still there after the breath? Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

The town of Gubbio has stopped going outside. A wolf, huge and fierce, has been killing animals in the fields, and people too. So anyone who leaves the walls goes armed, as if heading into battle, and plenty don't leave at all. Into this town walks a small man in a patched habit. He hears about the wolf, and he says he's going out to meet it. The people beg him not to. He makes the sign of the cross and walks out through the gate anyway, with a few companions trailing behind, and the townspeople climbing up wherever they can to watch. Today is a legend from the Little Flowers, and it's about what Francis says when the wolf comes running at him with its jaws open.
screen: `A TOWN AFRAID TO GO OUT.` → `A SMALL MAN WALKS TOWARD IT.` → `JAWS OPEN.`

segments.voice: The wolf charges. Francis makes the sign of the cross over it and calls it by a family name: Brother Wolf. Come here, he says, and in the name of Christ, do no harm to me or to anyone. And in the story the wolf closes its mouth, slows, and lies down at his feet like a lamb. Then Francis talks to it straight. You've done great harm, he says. You've killed God's creatures, and people made in God's image. The whole town is against you. But I want to make peace between you and them. And here is the turn that makes this more than a magic trick. Francis has noticed why the wolf kills. It's hungry. So the peace has two sides. The wolf will harm no one. And the town will feed the wolf for as long as it lives, so that hunger never drives it to harm anyone again. Francis asks for a pledge, holds out his hand, and the wolf lifts its paw and lays it in his palm. Then they walk into the town square together, and in front of everyone the bargain is made again, the people promising to feed it and the wolf giving its paw a second time. The story says the wolf went from door to door after that, and the people fed it kindly, and no dog barked at it. It's a legend, and people read it in more than one way. Some read a real animal and a real wonder. Some read a picture of a town and its enemy, a fierce man perhaps. Either way the shape is the same. Francis doesn't kill the wolf or chase it off. He gives it a brother's name, and he asks what it needs.
screen: `HE CALLS IT BROTHER WOLF.` · `THE WOLF KILLS BECAUSE IT'S HUNGRY.` · `A PAW LAID IN HIS HAND.` · `THE TOWN FEEDS ITS FORMER ENEMY.` · then, large: `BROTHER WOLF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make peace with a fear. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something that's been prowling around the edges of your life. A conversation you're dreading. A worry about money, or health, or someone you love. Don't run at it and don't run from it. Just let it come near, the way the wolf came near. Then ask it Francis's question. What does this fear actually want? Maybe it's hungry for something: safety, an answer, to be taken seriously. If a need shows itself, name it. If you pray, you can make the sign of the cross, as Francis did, and hold the fear before God. If you don't, simply breathe with it at arm's length, without a weapon. The bell holds the time.
The wolf of Gubbio. A legend of a hungry wolf, a frightened town, and a peace where each side gave something. Today's word.
Your line: brother wolf. Today, when something or someone feels like a threat, ask once what it might be hungry for before you decide what to do. Day one thousand two hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: The wolf of Gubbio is one of the stories told about Francis in the Little Flowers, and Catholics, especially Franciscans, retell it in sermons, art and children's books as a story of peacemaking.

match.prompt: the wolf and the town — tap the pairs.

myth: in the story, Francis drives the wolf out of Gubbio
he makes peace: the wolf harms no one, and the town feeds it.
Francis notices that the wolf kills out of hunger
so the peace has two sides: no more harm, and food for the wolf.
the pledge is made only once, outside the walls
the wolf gives its paw outside the town, then again in the square in front of everyone.

fork.setup: you're Francis. the wolf is lying at your feet, and the whole town hates it. what do you do?
options: tell the wolf to leave and never come back.
ask the town to feed it, if it harms no one.
let the townspeople decide its fate.
fork.reveal: Francis makes peace with two sides: the wolf promises no harm, and the town promises to feed it for life.

original.note: Italian, the language of the Little Flowers: brother wolf.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute story about a saint and a tame animal.
what it means: a peace where each side gives something: the wolf stops harming, the town stops letting it starve.
what a scholar hears: a legend in the Little Flowers, read by some as a wonder and by others as a picture of a town reconciled with an enemy.

sources.ref: Little Flowers of Saint Francis, ch. 21
sources.work: The Little Flowers of Saint Francis (Fioretti)

notes: The Fioretti chapter is paraphrased. Check: the wolf killing animals and people; townspeople going armed; Francis going out against their pleas with companions; the sign of the cross; 'Brother Wolf'; the rebuke for killing creatures and people made in God's image; the observation that the wolf did harm through hunger; the pledge with the paw, given outside and again in the square; the wolf going door to door, fed courteously, no dogs barking at it.
The Fioretti also says the wolf lived on in Gubbio for a time and died of old age, mourned by the town; omitted under the claims rule (no number of years given).
The 'fierce man' reading is offered as one way some readers take the legend; confirm this is fair to present.
Italian 'frate lupo' given as the original; confirm the Fioretti's form ('frate lupo').
Editor pass: the practice's generalization 'usually it's hungry for something' softened to 'maybe', so it no longer tells the listener what their fear wants.
